Name: Adam
Transcript: Thanks for doing this. There are no right or wrong answers, it's your experience I'm interested in, and we can stop whenever you like. So, to start. You've just taken on an allotment. What's that like for you, at the moment?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Honestly? Sceptical. Quite sceptical. My therapist suggested it, actually, which I'm aware is a sentence. She said, something with your hands, away from screens. And I laughed at her, a bit, which I felt bad about afterwards. But the thing is, I'd put my name down for a plot about three years ago, in a sort of self-improvement phase, and completely forgotten about it. And then two weeks after she said it, the email came. Plot fourteen is available, please confirm within seven days. So it felt like the universe was being a bit pointed. And I didn't feel I could turn down three years of waiting just because I was sceptical. So here I am. Sceptical, with a key.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Sceptical. Tell me more about that.

Name: Arlo
Transcript: It's the leaflet thing. You know when you're not doing great, and you go to the doctor, and you come out with a leaflet, and the leaflet says, have you tried a walk in nature? Have you tried gardening? And part of you wants to throw the leaflet in the bin, because, yes, obviously, I'll just go and look at a tree and my brain will stop doing the thing it does. So when she said it, it felt a bit like the leaflet. Like I'd become the sort of person who gets told to try gardening. I was signed off work for six weeks last autumn, so I suppose I am that sort of person now. That's quite hard to say out loud, actually.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You were signed off last autumn.

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Yeah. Burnout, panic attacks, the full set. I work in IT support for a software company. Second line. So my whole job is other people's problems, all day, in a queue. Something's broken, it's urgent, it was urgent yesterday, can you look at it. And I'm good at it, I'm actually very good at it, that's sort of the problem. I work from home, so it's just me and two screens and the queue, from eight till whenever. And one Tuesday in October I just couldn't open the laptop. I sat there looking at it with my hand on the lid. For about an hour. And that was that, for six weeks.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What were the six weeks like?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Strange. Very quiet and very loud at the same time. Quiet outside, loud inside. I didn't really leave the flat for the first two weeks. I watched a lot of things I don't remember. My sister came round with soup, which is something people do in films, I didn't know they did it in real life. And I kept checking my work email on my phone, which you're not supposed to do, my manager specifically said don't, and I did it every day, in bed, under the covers like a teenager. Just to see. The queue was still there. Someone else was doing it. It turned out the queue doesn't need me either. That was not as comforting as you'd think.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You work from home. What's that like?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Small. One bedroom, above a dry cleaner's, so it always smells slightly of other people's shirts. My desk is in the living room, so I live in my office, or I work in my living room, depending on how you look at it. I can see the laptop from the sofa, and from the bed if the door's open. I keep the door shut now. That was a therapy thing too. Shut the bedroom door so you can't see the laptop. It helps, a bit. The plot's the first place in two years that doesn't have the laptop in it somewhere.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What do you hope the plot might do?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Quiet my head, I suppose. If I'm allowed one hope. It's very loud in there, most of the time. It's like having forty tabs open and one of them is playing music and you can't find which one. So I want one problem that's just soil and weather. That nobody can email me about. That doesn't have a ticket number. Do you know what I mean? A problem that isn't anyone's and doesn't escalate. If the carrots fail, nobody's going to put it in my appraisal. That's the dream, really. A problem with no one attached to it.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Have you been down yet?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Twice. I read four books first, which is very me. Four books, and I watched about nine hours of videos. I made a spreadsheet. Sowing dates, colour-coded by month, with a column for what I'd actually sown and a column for the difference. I was quite proud of the spreadsheet. And then I got there, and the books were no use at all. None. The soil was nothing like the pictures. In the pictures it's this crumbly brown stuff, like chocolate cake. Mine is clay. Wet, grey, heavy clay. It stuck to the fork like it had opinions. I'd lift a forkful and the fork would come up and the clay wouldn't.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What was that like?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Annoying, then funny. Mostly annoying, at first. I stood there in brand new gloves, still with the label on, they had a little cardboard tag, and I felt like a complete fraud. Like I was cosplaying a gardener. And there's an old man on the next plot, Des, he must be eighty, he's got a flat cap and a shed covered in old number plates, and he'd been watching me. Just leaning on his fork, watching me fight the clay. And after about twenty minutes he said, everyone feels like that the first year. And most of the second. And then he went back to his digging.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Everyone feels like that the first year.

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Which was either kind or a threat, I genuinely couldn't tell. I went home and thought about it for most of the evening. Was he being nice? Was he saying I'm doing it wrong? Was he saying I won't last? I'm like that with people at the moment. I read everything as an evaluation. Everyone's a performance review. He probably just meant, everyone feels like that the first year. He probably didn't think about it again. I thought about it for about four hours.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You said you're like that with people at the moment.

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Yeah. I'm fine on calls. I'm very good on calls, actually, I'm calm, I'm reassuring, I've got a voice for it. But in person I don't really know where to put myself any more. Since being off, mostly. I've sort of lost the habit of people who aren't on a screen. I don't know what to do with my face. On a call you can mute yourself and pull a face and unmute. In real life there's no mute. So at the plot I mostly just put my head down and hope nobody comes over. Which is probably the opposite of what my therapist had in mind.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What was the digging like, in your body?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Oh, terrible. And kind of amazing. I've been living from the neck up for about ten years, I think. My body's basically a thing that carries my head to the desk. And after the first two hours digging, I had blisters on both hands, through the new gloves, and my back was screaming, and that night I couldn't sleep from the ache. Just lay there aching. And then the next night I slept nine hours. Nine. I haven't slept nine hours since university. But the strange thing, the thing I keep thinking about, is that it was the first time in months I knew where my hands were.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Knew where your hands were. What's that like?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: It's hard to explain. At work my hands are just, input devices. They're the bit between my brain and the keyboard. I don't notice them. At the plot they were cold and they were sore and there was clay under the nails that wouldn't come out, and they were mine. They were definitely mine. I kept looking at them on the bus home. Turning them over. Like they'd been away somewhere and come back. Which is slightly embarrassing to say to someone with a recorder.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You said your body's a thing that carries your head to the desk.

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Yeah. I mean, I went to the gym for a bit, last year. But that was also a spreadsheet, reps and sets and a graph. My body was a project there too. At the plot it wasn't a project, it was just there, doing the digging. I wasn't measuring it. I couldn't, really, you can't measure digging clay, it's just horrible and then you stop. And I think that's partly why I noticed my hands. Because I wasn't measuring them. They weren't data. They were just sore.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And the spreadsheet?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Yeah. So I showed it to my therapist. Proudly. And she looked at it for a while and she said, quite gently, so you've turned the thing that was meant to be not work into a project with a timeline. And I said, it's not a timeline, it's a sowing schedule. And she just looked at me. And she was right. Obviously. That's exactly the thing. That's what I do. I can see myself doing it, I can watch myself doing it from about three feet away, and I still do it. Knowing doesn't stop it. It just means I get to watch.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What's at stake for you in it, would you say?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Not failing, I suppose. That's the honest answer. The six weeks off felt like failing. Everybody was very nice about it, work was very nice about it, but it felt like failing. Like I'd broken in public. And I really don't want this to be another thing I fail at. With an audience.

Name: Adam
Transcript: With an audience?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: At the plot everything's visible. That's the thing I hadn't thought about. Everybody can see everybody's plot. You walk up the path and you can see who's on top of it and who isn't. At work you can hide a mistake in a log file, nobody reads the logs. Here your mistakes are just out there, in rows, for anyone who walks past. Des can see my clay from his shed. The whole site can see my clay. It's a very public way to be bad at something.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What would it mean, if it was another thing you failed at?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: That last autumn wasn't a one-off. That's what I'm scared of, I think, if I'm being properly honest. At the moment I can tell myself it was a blip. A bad patch, I recovered, I'm back at work, all good. But if I can't even do this, if I can't even look after a vegetable patch that my therapist more or less prescribed, then maybe it wasn't a blip. Maybe that's just what I'm like now. Maybe I'm someone who breaks. And I'd rather not find that out in front of Des.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What do you picture the year being like?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: I try not to picture it. My therapist says don't set targets, let it be what it is. So I haven't set targets. Except I have, obviously. I've set one. I want to still be going in October. That's it. That's the only target. Still turning up in October. That's the key performance indicator. I'm aware that's a joke and not a joke.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What do you picture yourself doing there, on a good day?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Honestly, nothing. That's the picture. Me, on a fold-up chair, at the end of a row of something green, not doing anything, not thinking about anything, and not feeling guilty about not doing anything. That's the fantasy. Which is ridiculous, because I've just told you I made a spreadsheet. But the picture in my head isn't the spreadsheet. The picture is the chair. I just don't know how you get from the spreadsheet to the chair. Maybe that's what the year is for.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Is there anything else about it, at the moment, that I haven't asked about?

Name: Arlo
Transcript: Can I add one thing? The first time I went, the very first time, with the key, I sat in the car in the car park for twenty minutes before I got out. I don't really know why. There were two people at the gate talking, and I waited until they'd gone. I just sat there with the engine off, pretending to look at my phone. Twenty minutes. Then they went, and I got out. I think about that quite a lot. It was a bit of a low moment, if I'm honest. Sitting in a car park, hiding from two people with a flask.
